title: Coloured bin lids (South Jutland)
description: Waste bins vary by area in Denmark. Bins with green, purple and yellow lids are found in southern Jutland, roughly south of a line from Blåvand to Brande and Vejle and west of the Little Belt, down to the German border.

title: Letter tubes (Jutland)
description: Tube-shaped mailboxes mounted on a post are typical of Jutland and help tell it apart from the Danish islands.

title: Place names ending in '-inge', '-tofte', '-bølle' (the islands)
description: In Fyn and Sjælland the suffixes -ing, -toft and -bøl tend to take an extra '-e': -inge, -tofte, -bølle. This very reliably divides Denmark between the mainland and the islands. -bølle (like -bøl) is generally only found in the south of its region.

title: Place names ending in '-ing', '-toft', '-bøl' (Jylland)
description: On the mainland the suffixes keep their short form: -ing, -toft, -bøl, whereas Fyn and Sjælland add an '-e' (-inge, -tofte, -bølle). -bøl is generally only found in the south of Jylland.

title: Place names ending in '-have'
description: One of the suffixes unique to, or very rarely found outside, the region made of Fyn, the islands south of Sjælland and the coast of Jylland adjacent to Fyn. The map shows where towns with this ending are found (the author's suffix maps).

description: One of the few suffixes unique to Jylland. The map shows where towns with this ending are found (the author's suffix maps).

description: One of the few suffixes unique to Jylland. The map shows where towns with this ending are found (the author's suffix maps).

title: Place names ending in '-marke' (Møn)
description: The suffix '-marke' is very common on Møn, with a couple of exceptions on nearby Lolland.

title: Place names ending in '-sker' (Bornholm)
description: The suffix '-sker' is unique to Bornholm.

title: Monosyllabic town names (western central Jylland)
description: Monosyllabic town names with no ending at all are very common in western central Jylland (the red area): Tim, No, Vemb, Tvis, Hjerm… They can sometimes also be found in other parts of north and central Jutland, and very rarely on Sjælland.

title: Dead-flat fields with poplars (Lolland, Falster)
description: Dead-flat agricultural landscape (as opposed to the very gently rolling fields of most of the country) combined with poplar trees, which are very distinct and not found in most of Denmark. Also applies to Falster and, to a lesser extent, adjacent coastal areas of Sjælland.

title: Flat, treeless Wadden Sea landscape
description: In the south-west corner of the country lies the Wadden Sea, mostly within Vadehavet national park: one of the only areas with dead-flat landscapes and no trees. Cow and sheep herds can be found here (otherwise very rare), as well as occasional heaths, particularly on Rømø. Similarly flat, treeless landscapes are found a little further north around Ringkøbing Fjord.

title: Raised grassy dune along the west coast
description: A distinct raised, grassy dune runs along almost the entire west coast of the country; it is not found on other coastlines. Along some stretches it looks less like a single dune and more like a cluster of dunes on the west side of the road.

title: Klitter dune landscape
description: 'Klitter' is a type of landscape popular with holidaymakers: a mess of irregular dunes and shrubs such as sea buckthorn. Mainly found on the west side of Ringkøbing Fjord (Holmsland Klit), less so on Skagen Odde and in Thy national park.

title: Limfjord: farmland, canola and wind turbines
description: Limfjord is an island of agriculture in an otherwise fairly fallow region: crops otherwise found in the south-east grow here (canola, rye). It also has the highest density of wind turbines in the country. Best identified by a combination of canola, wind turbines, hilly terrain and, above all, overcast coverage.

title: Heaths and barren fields (west Midtjylland)
description: The western half of Midtjylland is the least densely populated part of Denmark and looks quite barren: lots of fallow fields and grass fields, but most uniquely heaths — tall grass and heather (bushes of tiny pink-purple flowers), often interspersed with trees.

title: Vejle, the city surrounded by hills
description: Vejle is the only city in Denmark surrounded by hills, visible from most of its coverage.

title: Djursland's steep, undulating hills
description: Djursland (the peninsula on the east coast of Jylland) is not home to the highest hills in the country, but has the most visibly hilly terrain: steep and undulating. Hilly shorelines also point to Djursland, though they can be found further south along the Jylland coast too.

title: Wheat fields (south-east)
description: Wheat fields are generally more common in the south-east of the country (the maps show wheat and barley).

title: Beetroot fields (Lolland, Falster, SW Sjælland)
description: Beetroot crops are an even more precise indicator of the south-east: they are found primarily on Lolland, Falster and parts of south-western Sjælland.

title: Christmas tree plantations
description: Denmark is the world's largest producer of Christmas trees, especially Nordmann firs. The highest concentrations of plantations are around Mariager Fjord and the highlands around Silkeborg, but they can generally be found in the areas circled in green (precise data is hard to come by).

title: Large patches of butterbur (Sjælland)
description: Butterbur is a very distinctive weed commonly found by the roadside. It becomes more common the further south-east you go; large patches like this one are rarely found outside Sjælland.

title: Coniferous forests (north-west)
description: There is a north-west to south-east gradient: coniferous trees are more prevalent in the north-west and broadleaf trees dominate the south-east. Hill country can disturb this gradient somewhat.

title: Bornholm flag
description: Bornholm has a strong local character and will occasionally fly its own flag: red with a green Nordic cross. You won't see it often, but it is easy to remember.

title: Ærø flag
description: Ærø will occasionally fly its own flag: yellow, green and red horizontal stripes. Yes, it is the same as Lithuania's.

title: Creative town entry signs (Vendsyssel)
description: In Vendsyssel (the far north of Denmark) town entry signs are often more creative: twin Danish flagpoles next to the entry signs (sometimes without the flags), house-shaped signs, and many other less categorisable designs. (Fyn's 'washboard' signs are a separate, already documented meta.)

title: Folded sign backs (Midtjylland, islands south of Sjælland)
description: EXPERIMENTAL. Danish road signs are flat with no border by default. Folded sign backs — also recognisable from the front by a slight metal border — are really only common in Midtjylland (the cluster extends slightly into neighbouring regions) and on the islands south of Sjælland; rarely in the rest of Sjælland. Use with caution: there may be many exceptions.

title: Crown emblem: national parks
description: A crown emblem on a brown background means you are in one of Denmark's five national parks. The two on Sjælland are very small with almost no roads, so assume one of the three in Jylland: Thy and the Wadden Sea (dunes, coastal vegetation) or, if not, Mols Bjerge on Djursland.

title: Marguerite Route daisy signs
description: Little daisy symbols on road signs mark the Marguerite Route, which covers the most beautiful parts of the country. It goes almost everywhere, but it rules out Bornholm, and it is denser on Fyn, around Limfjord, etc.

title: Legoland signs and Lego references (Billund)
description: Lego comes from Billund, home of Legoland. Most road signs in the area give directions to Legoland, and there are other Lego references throughout the town.
